blocks.text: Motivation, rewards, and healthy player return
The reward philosophy of Symphony of Justice should begin with one principle:
A meaningful reward does not merely increase a number. It should recognize an action, unlock a possibility, preserve a memory, or bring the player closer to a goal that matters to them.
The system should primarily reward six behaviors:
A player who leaves the main path to investigate a ruin, solve a puzzle, or find a hidden place should feel that their curiosity had value.
This aligns with the historical exploration missions, which were specifically designed to uncover parts of the world, their origins, and past events.
The player should be rewarded for learning:
Building a different composition, developing another character, or using a new strategy should have value, especially in Endgame.
should produce rewards of its own.
Participating Regularly Without Turning It into an Obligation
Recurring activities can reward returning, but they should not make taking a break feel like a mistake.
A reward can be meaningful if it fulfills at least one of these functions:
POWER Improves what the player can do.
POSSIBILITY Enables a new build, character, composition, or interaction.
KNOWLEDGE Reveals something new about the world.
EXPRESSION Allows the player to represent preferences or achievements.
RECOGNITION Shows that the player overcame something difficult.
PROGRESS Brings the player closer to a larger goal.
We do not want 27 different items appearing after every battle simply to manufacture an artificial sense of reward.
It is better for the player to understand what they obtained and why it matters.
The player knows approximately what they will receive.
Discoveries, special drops, cosmetics, or small secrets. These create excitement. Important progression should not depend exclusively on this second category.
The reward should reinforce the activity that produced it.

Exploration rewards discovery, Bosses reward mastery. Stories reward knowledge, Endgame rewards specialization, and Gacha rewards collection. This prevents absolutely everything from ultimately handing out the exact same sack of coins.

Therefore: discovering the truth is also a reward.

Ideally, they should not provide significant power. Social recognition works best when another player can see it and understand: “That person earned this by doing X.”

The historical documentation already has a strong philosophy for daily activities: Hunts should not force the player to complete a specific checklist. Different activities grant points that accumulate up to a maximum, allowing the player to choose what to do. The later presentation preserves exactly this logic of accumulation through objectives with different values.
That philosophy should also be applied to rewards.

They should not contain an exclusive character or weapon that is impossible to obtain later.
The historical documentation already explicitly includes weekly activities within Endgame.
They do not need to be played all on the same day.
We can later implement one or more systems.
Up to a certain number of daily objectives may accumulate.
For example: you did not play today → tomorrow it resets, and the Daily is lost.
Part of the daily rewards may also be obtained through weekly progress.
Participating in an event counts simultaneously toward daily/weekly objectives.
This prevents: event + dailies + weekly + farming
from functioning like four separate jobs.
I do not recommend making the main reward depend only on: open the game → claim → close.
An occasional calendar may exist, but it should not become the main retention strategy.
Achievements should recognize actions that demonstrate:
They should not simply become a second quest list.
Defeat a specific Boss after breaking all of its protections.
Trigger a specified number of different reactions.
I would not recommend: “Obtain every 5★ character.”
because it turns spending or luck into a supposed achievement of skill.

The historical Library was already conceived as a database that expands as the protagonist discovers enemies, abilities, strengths, and fragments of lore. This makes it possible to integrate Achievements perfectly with discovery.
Avoid achievements that force players to: add one hundred strangers or perform artificial interactions.
They work particularly well when they do not grant significant power.
Difficult achievements should especially reward: recognition and expression.
An extremely difficult achievement may grant: a visually recognizable cosmetic.
This allows the player to display what they achieved without creating a statistical advantage.
A general achievement score may exist, but it should be informational.
It does not need to become another competitive progression system.
The motivation to return should work across several time scales.
We do not want the entire answer to be: “Come back because something disappears tomorrow.”
We want to combine: CONTINUITY + CURIOSITY + PROGRESSION + VARIETY + COMMUNITY
The Game Vision already envisions an experience that can expand through new regions, characters, stories, activities, and systems.
The player knows: “I need two more materials to evolve Juro.”

The motivation should be: “I have something interesting to do.”
Not: “My reward disappears on Sunday at 11:59 PM.”
Why Return in a New Version
This is where Live Content comes in:
The historical documentation already intended each update to introduce events capable of varying the experience.
These are especially important because they remain even when there is no new content.
Says: “There is something new to experience.”
Says: “I still have something of my own that I want to achieve.”
Healthy retention needs both. If we depend only on updates, the game feels empty between versions. If we depend only on permanent farming, it becomes static.
For someone returning after several months:
They should not open the game and receive: seventeen pop-ups, nine new currencies, and three people shouting that everything ends tomorrow.
Here we need to be very clear: the original documents include temporary events and update-based content, but they do not define an Anti-FOMO policy.

9. No Critical Rewards Behind Tiny Time Windows
Avoid: “Exclusive Boss available only Tuesday from 6:00 PM to 8:00 PM.”
Activities should provide sufficiently wide participation windows.
10. Do Not Penalize Late Event Starts
If a player starts the event during its final week, they should still be able to reasonably complete its story. We can use:
but once content is released, earlier content remains available until the event ends.
11. No Wasted Stamina as Psychological Punishment
We should not design interfaces that constantly remind the player: “Your energy is full, you are wasting progress.”
Energy, if it exists for certain activities, should function as an economic tool, not as a guilt alarm.
12. No Sales Based on Withholding Information
Do not use fake resettable timers.
As already proposed in the Gacha System, pity and guarantees should carry over between compatible Banners. Ending a version should not erase prior investment.
The Legacy Card may expand a character. It should not create: “get them six times before they disappear or they will remain useless.” The first copy should provide a fully functional character.
This can become the core Anti-FOMO idea: Symphony of Justice should assume that its players have lives outside the game.
Returning after a week should produce: curiosity about what happened
and not: anxiety about everything that was missed.
